questions.question: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a describes:
options: The value f(a) exactly
Where the values of f(x) head near a, regardless of f(a)
The steepest point of the graph
The area under the curve
questions.rationale: Limits look at the approach: values of f(x) can settle toward L near a even when f(a) itself is undefined or different.

questions.question: Evaluate: lim(x→1) (x² − 1)/(x − 1)
options: Does not exist
questions.rationale: Factor and cancel: ((x−1)(x+1))/(x−1) = x + 1 for x ≠ 1, which approaches 2 as x → 1.

questions.question: For the two-sided limit to exist at a point, which must be true?
options: f(a) must equal zero
Left-hand and right-hand limits must agree
The function must be increasing
The graph must have an asymptote
questions.rationale: Both one-sided limits must be equal; if they disagree (a jump), the two-sided limit does not exist.

questions.question: A function is continuous at x = a exactly when:
options: It is defined everywhere on the real line
f(a) exists, the limit exists, and they are equal
Its derivative is positive there
The graph is a straight line
questions.rationale: Continuity needs all three: defined value, existing limit, and both matching — informally, no pen-lift at that point.

questions.question: The derivative — calculus's measure of instantaneous change — is formally defined as:
options: A limit of average rates over shrinking intervals
An infinite sum of rectangles
The slope of any secant line
A type of asymptote
questions.rationale: Derivatives are limits of difference quotients [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h as h → 0; integrals are the ones built from sums of thin rectangles.

questions.question: What does the difference quotient [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h measure?
options: The exact instantaneous speed at x
An average rate over an interval of width h
The area under f between x and x+h
A one-sided limit from the left
questions.rationale: It is an average rate over the interval from x to x+h; only as h shrinks toward 0 does the fraction approach the instantaneous rate.

questions.question: Why is f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) undefined at x = 1?
options: Because the numerator x² − 1 equals 0 there
Because substituting x = 1 gives division by zero
Because the values grow without bound near every point
Because the graph has a vertical asymptote at x = 0
questions.rationale: At x = 1 both numerator and denominator vanish, giving 0/0 (division by zero); yet for x ≠ 1 the expression simplifies to x + 1, so its limit is still 2.

questions.question: If the values of f(x) grow without bound as x → a, what happens to the limit?
options: It exists and equals some large finite number
It does not exist as a number — we say the limit is infinite
It automatically equals f(a)
It always equals zero
questions.rationale: Unbounded growth means no single value L is approached, so the limit fails to exist as a number — informally we say the limit is infinite.

questions.question: Which calculus object is defined as a limit of sums of infinitely many thin rectangles?
options: The derivative
The integral
A difference quotient
A secant slope
questions.rationale: Integrals are limits of sums of infinitely many thin rectangles, which give areas; derivatives come from limits of difference quotients.

questions.question: The right-hand limit, written x → a⁺, describes:
options: Approaching a from above (values greater than a)
Approaching a from below (values less than a)
Evaluating f(a) directly
Letting h become negative infinity
questions.rationale: x → a⁺ approaches a from above while x → a⁻ approaches from below; the two-sided limit exists only when these two agree.
